claim: Glutamate transporters reside in the plasma membranes of glial cells and neurons.
source: Glutamate transporters, or excitatory amino acid transporters (EAATs), reside in the plasma membranes of glial cells and neurons, where they catalyze the re-uptake of the neurotransmitters glutamate and aspartate (L-asp) (Danbolt, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Danbolt, 2001

claim: EAATs catalyze the re-uptake of the neurotransmitters glutamate and aspartate.
source: Glutamate transporters, or excitatory amino acid transporters (EAATs), reside in the plasma membranes of glial cells and neurons, where they catalyze the re-uptake of the neurotransmitters glutamate and aspartate (L-asp) (Danbolt, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Danbolt, 2001

claim: EAATs terminate neurotransmission events supporting memory formation and cognition.
source: EAATs terminate neurotransmission events supporting memory formation and cognition, and also prevent excitotoxicity caused by overstimulation of glutamate receptors.
evidence: Statement of established function in the text

claim: EAATs prevent excitotoxicity caused by overstimulation of glutamate receptors.
source: EAATs terminate neurotransmission events supporting memory formation and cognition, and also prevent excitotoxicity caused by overstimulation of glutamate receptors.
evidence: Statement of established function in the text

claim: Dysfunction of EAATs is linked to neurological disorders, poor recovery from stroke and traumatic brain injuries.
source: Dysfunction of EAATs is linked to neurological disorders, poor recovery from stroke and traumatic brain injuries (Yi and Hazell, 2006; Sheldon and Robinson, 2007; Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yi and Hazell, 2006; Sheldon and Robinson, 2007; Kim et al., 2013

claim: EAATs transport one substrate molecule together with three sodium ions and one proton.
source: To maintain steep trans-membrane glutamate gradients, EAATs transport one substrate molecule together with three sodium ions (Na+) and one proton.
evidence: Statement of established transport stoichiometry in the text

claim: After release of substrate and ions into the cytoplasm, counter-transport of one potassium ion resets the transporter for the next cycle.
source: After their release into the cytoplasm, counter-transport of one potassium ion (K+) resets the transporter for the next cycle (Zerangue and Kavanaugh, 1996; Levy et al., 1998; Owe et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zerangue and Kavanaugh, 1996; Levy et al., 1998; Owe et al., 2006

claim: GltPh is an archaeal homologue from Pyrococcus horikoshii that symports L-asp together with three Na+ ions.
source: Key mechanistic and structural insights into this family of transporters come from studies on an archaeal homologue from Pyrococcus horikoshii, GltPh (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which symports L-asp together with three Na+ ions (Groeneveld and Slotboom, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Groeneveld and Slotboom, 2010

claim: GltPh shows no dependence on counter-transport of K+ under the conditions tested.
source: however, it shows no dependence on counter-transport of K+ under the conditions tested (Ryan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2009

claim: GltPh is a homo-trimer.
source: GltPh, like EAATs, is a homo-trimer (Gendreau et al., 2004; Yernool et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gendreau et al., 2004; Yernool et al., 2004

claim: Each protomer of GltPh consists of a central scaffolding trimerization domain and a peripheral transport domain containing the substrate and ion binding sites.
source: Each protomer consists of a central scaffolding trimerization domain and a peripheral transport domain containing the substrate and ion binding sites (Boudker et al., 2007; Reyes et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boudker et al., 2007; Reyes et al., 2009

claim: When bound to Na+ and L-asp, each transport domain moves by ∼15 Å across the membrane from an outward- to an inward-facing position.
source: When bound to Na+ and L-asp ('fully bound' from here on), each transport domain moves by ∼15 Å across the membrane from an outward- to an inward-facing position, in which the substrate binding site is near the extracellular solution and the cytoplasm, respectively (Reyes et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reyes et al., 2009

claim: Structurally symmetric helical hairpins HP1 and HP2 occlude the bound substrate from the solvent and are thought to serve as gates.
source: Structurally symmetric helical hairpins, HP1 and HP2, occlude the bound substrate from the solvent and are thought to serve as gates (Boudker et al., 2007; Huang and Tajkhorshid, 2008; Shrivastava et al., 2008; Reyes et al., 2009; DeChancie et al., 2010; Focke et al., 2011; Zomot and Bahar, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Two Na+-binding sites (Na1 and Na2) were identified crystallographically using thallium.
source: Two Na+-binding sites (Na1 and Na2), neither of which directly coordinates the substrate, were identified crystallographically using thallium (Tl+) (Boudker et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boudker et al., 2007

claim: Neither Na1 nor Na2 directly coordinates the substrate.
source: Two Na+-binding sites (Na1 and Na2), neither of which directly coordinates the substrate, were identified crystallographically using thallium (Tl+) (Boudker et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boudker et al., 2007

claim: The location of the third Na+-binding site is being debated.
source: The location of the third Na+-binding site is being debated (Holley and Kavanaugh, 2009; Huang and Tajkhorshid, 2010; Larsson et al., 2010; Tao et al., 2010; Bastug et al., 2012; Teichman et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies with different proposals

claim: A highly conserved non-helical Asn310-Met311-Asp312 (NMD) motif interrupts trans-membrane segment (TM) 7.
source: A highly conserved non-helical Asn310-Met311-Asp312 (NMD) motif interrupts trans-membrane segment (TM) 7 (see below).
evidence: Statement of structural feature in the text

claim: The NMD motif lines the back of the substrate- and ion-binding sites and is involved in binding of the ligands.
source: It lines the back of the substrate- and ion-binding sites and is involved in binding of the ligands (Rosental et al., 2006; Tao et al., 2006; Rosental and Kanner, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rosental et al., 2006; Tao et al., 2006; Rosental and Kanner, 2010

claim: The main chain carbonyl oxygen of Asn310 contributes to Na1 site.
source: The main chain carbonyl oxygen of Asn310 contributes to Na1 site, while the side chain of Met311 protrudes between the substrate, Na1 and Na2 binding sites (Boudker et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boudker et al., 2007

claim: The side chain of Met311 protrudes between the substrate, Na1 and Na2 binding sites.
source: The main chain carbonyl oxygen of Asn310 contributes to Na1 site, while the side chain of Met311 protrudes between the substrate, Na1 and Na2 binding sites (Boudker et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boudker et al., 2007

claim: Symport requires that neither the substrate nor the ions alone are efficiently transported.
source: Symport requires that neither the substrate nor the ions alone are efficiently transported (Crane, 1977).
evidence: Supported by citation to Crane, 1977

claim: To traverse the membrane, the transport domains of GltPh and EAATs must be loaded with both Na+ ions and substrate.
source: Therefore to traverse the membrane, the transport domains of GltPh and EAATs must be loaded with both Na+ ions and substrate.
evidence: Logical inference from symport requirement

claim: To complete the transport cycle, the transport domain of GltPh must translocate readily when it is free of both solutes (apo).
source: To complete the transport cycle, the transport domain of GltPh must also translocate readily when it is free of both solutes (apo), while in EAATs it requires binding of a K+ ion.
evidence: Logical inference from transport cycle requirements

claim: In EAATs, completion of the transport cycle requires binding of a K+ ion.
source: To complete the transport cycle, the transport domain of GltPh must also translocate readily when it is free of both solutes (apo), while in EAATs it requires binding of a K+ ion.
evidence: Logical inference from transport cycle requirements and known EAAT properties

claim: The apo transport domain shows identical structures when facing outward or inward.
source: We find that the apo transport domain shows identical structures when facing outward or inward.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data presented in the study

claim: While ligand-binding sites are distorted in the apo form, the domain remains compact.
source: While ligand-binding sites are distorted, the domain remains compact, suggesting that it relocates across the membrane as a rigid body, similarly to when it is fully bound (Reyes et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data and comparison to previous structures

claim: The apo transport domain relocates across the membrane as a rigid body, similarly to when it is fully bound.
source: While ligand-binding sites are distorted, the domain remains compact, suggesting that it relocates across the membrane as a rigid body, similarly to when it is fully bound (Reyes et al., 2009).
evidence: Inference from structural data and comparison to previous work

claim: Ion binding to Na1 site triggers structural changes that are propagated to the extracellular gate HP2.
source: Ion binding to Na1 site, located deep in the core of the transport domain, triggers structural changes that are propagated to the extracellular gate HP2, at least in part, by the side chain of Met311 in the NMD motif.
evidence: Supported by comparison of apo and ion-bound structures

claim: Structural changes upon Na+ binding are propagated to HP2 at least in part by the side chain of Met311 in the NMD motif.
source: Ion binding to Na1 site, located deep in the core of the transport domain, triggers structural changes that are propagated to the extracellular gate HP2, at least in part, by the side chain of Met311 in the NMD motif.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis and mutagenesis data

claim: Upon Na+ binding, HP2 frees the substrate binding and Na2 sites, assuming conformations more similar to the fully bound transporter.
source: Consequently HP2, which in the apo form is collapsed into the substrate binding and Na2 sites, frees the sites, assuming conformations more similar to the conformation observed in the fully bound transporter.
evidence: Supported by comparison of apo, Na+-bound, and fully bound structures

claim: Na+-dependent structural changes underlie the high cooperativity of Na+ and substrate binding.
source: We suggest that these Na+-dependent structural changes underlie the high cooperativity of Na+ and substrate binding, which is thought to be one of the key coupling mechanisms (Reyes et al., 2013).
evidence: Hypothesis based on structural data and previous functional studies

claim: In the structure of Na+-bound outward-facing GltPh, opening of HP2 tip is observed.
source: Furthermore, in the structure of Na+-bound outward-facing GltPh we observe opening of HP2 tip, which may facilitate L-asp access to its binding site and prevent the inward movement of the Na+-only bound transport domain, as previously suggested (Focke et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data

claim: Opening of HP2 tip may facilitate L-asp access to its binding site.
source: Furthermore, in the structure of Na+-bound outward-facing GltPh we observe opening of HP2 tip, which may facilitate L-asp access to its binding site and prevent the inward movement of the Na+-only bound transport domain, as previously suggested (Focke et al., 2011).
evidence: Speculation based on structural observation and previous suggestion

claim: Opening of HP2 tip may prevent the inward movement of the Na+-only bound transport domain.
source: Furthermore, in the structure of Na+-bound outward-facing GltPh we observe opening of HP2 tip, which may facilitate L-asp access to its binding site and prevent the inward movement of the Na+-only bound transport domain, as previously suggested (Focke et al., 2011).
evidence: Speculation based on structural observation and previous suggestion

claim: Soaks of apo GltPh crystals in Tl+ reveal new cation-binding sites within the apo-like protein architecture.
source: Remarkably, soaks of apo GltPh crystals in Tl+ reveal new cation-binding sites within the apo-like protein architecture.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data from Tl+ soaking experiments

claim: One new cation-binding site overlaps with the substrate-binding site.
source: One such site overlaps with the substrate-binding site.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data

claim: Binding of a cation to the Ct site would compete with binding of Na+ and the transported substrate.
source: Because binding of a cation to this site would compete with binding of Na+ and the transported substrate, it is well suited to serve as a binding site for a counter-transported ion.
evidence: Inference from structural overlap of binding sites

claim: The Ct site is well suited to serve as a binding site for a counter-transported ion.
source: Because binding of a cation to this site would compete with binding of Na+ and the transported substrate, it is well suited to serve as a binding site for a counter-transported ion.
evidence: Speculation based on structural properties of the site

claim: The closed translocation-competent conformation of the transport domain free of Na+ and substrate is intrinsically stable in GltPh but not in EAATs.
source: We propose that the closed translocation-competent conformation of the transport domain free of Na+ and substrate is intrinsically stable in GltPh but not in EAATs, in which K+ binding at the newly identified site is required, coupling transport cycle completion to K+ counter-transport.
evidence: Hypothesis based on structural data and functional differences between GltPh and EAATs

claim: In EAATs, K+ binding at the newly identified site is required to stabilize the translocation-competent conformation, coupling transport cycle completion to K+ counter-transport.
source: We propose that the closed translocation-competent conformation of the transport domain free of Na+ and substrate is intrinsically stable in GltPh but not in EAATs, in which K+ binding at the newly identified site is required, coupling transport cycle completion to K+ counter-transport.
evidence: Hypothesis based on structural data and functional differences between GltPh and EAATs

claim: GltPh-R397A shows a drastically decreased affinity for substrate.
source: To determine the structure of apo GltPh, we used R397A mutant that shows a drastically decreased affinity for substrate (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by ITC data shown in Figure 1A

claim: When fully bound, GltPh-R397A crystallizes in the outward-facing state, like wild type GltPh.
source: When fully bound, GltPh-R397A crystallizes in the outward-facing state, like wild type GltPh, except that L-asp coordination is slightly altered because the mutant is missing the key coordinating side chain of Arg397 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Bendahan et al., 2000; Boudker et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data and comparison to wild type

claim: In GltPh-R397A, L-asp coordination is slightly altered because the mutant is missing the key coordinating side chain of Arg397.
source: When fully bound, GltPh-R397A crystallizes in the outward-facing state, like wild type GltPh, except that L-asp coordination is slightly altered because the mutant is missing the key coordinating side chain of Arg397 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Bendahan et al., 2000; Boudker et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 1B

claim: R397A is suitable to capture the apo and ions-only bound outward-facing states for structural characterization.
source: These results suggest that R397A is suitable to capture the apo and ions-only bound outward-facing states for their structural characterization.
evidence: Inference from structural similarity to wild type when fully bound

claim: Removal of Arg397 may affect local electrostatics, potentially altering ion binding.
source: However, removal of Arg397 may affect local electrostatics, potentially altering ion binding; thus these studies should be interpreted with caution.
evidence: Speculation about potential effects of the mutation

claim: Apo GltPh-R397A crystallized in an outward-facing conformation that is similar to the structure reported for a close GltPh homologue.
source: Apo GltPh-R397A also crystallized in an outward-facing conformation that is similar to the structure reported for a close GltPh homologue (Jensen et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data and comparison to previous structure

claim: The positions and orientations of the transport domains relative to the trimerization domains remain essentially unchanged in the apo and fully bound forms of GltPh-R397A and GltPhin.
source: The positions and orientations of the transport domains relative to the trimerization domains remain essentially unchanged in the apo and fully bound forms of GltPh-R397A and GltPhin (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2

claim: The conformations of the transport domains themselves differ significantly between apo and fully bound forms.
source: In contrast, the conformations of the transport domains themselves differ significantly.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison

claim: The apo conformations of the transport domain are nearly identical in the outward- and inward-facing states.
source: Most remarkably, the apo conformations of the transport domain are nearly identical in the outward- and inward-facing states (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3A and supplements

claim: The apo conformation of the transport domain is independent of the transport domain orientations and crystal packing environments.
source: Most remarkably, the apo conformations of the transport domain are nearly identical in the outward- and inward-facing states (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) and are therefore independent of the transport domain orientations and crystal packing environments.
evidence: Inference from identical structures in different crystal forms

claim: The conformational differences between fully bound and apo forms include a concerted movement of HP2 and TM8a.
source: The conformational differences between fully bound and apo forms of the transport domain include a concerted movement of HP2 and TM8a, which form the extracellular surface of the domain, and local rearrangements at the ligand binding sites, involving HP2, the NMD motif and TM3 (Figure 3B–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in figures

claim: The conformational differences between fully bound and apo forms include local rearrangements at the ligand binding sites, involving HP2, the NMD motif and TM3.
source: The conformational differences between fully bound and apo forms of the transport domain include a concerted movement of HP2 and TM8a, which form the extracellular surface of the domain, and local rearrangements at the ligand binding sites, involving HP2, the NMD motif and TM3 (Figure 3B–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in figures

claim: In HP2, the last helical turn of HP2a unwinds in the apo form.
source: In HP2, the last helical turn of HP2a unwinds, and HP2a together with the loop region at HP2 tip collapse into the substrate and Na2 binding sites.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison

claim: In the apo form, HP2a together with the loop region at HP2 tip collapse into the substrate and Na2 binding sites.
source: In HP2, the last helical turn of HP2a unwinds, and HP2a together with the loop region at HP2 tip collapse into the substrate and Na2 binding sites.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison

claim: Within the NMD motif, the side chain of Asn310 rotates away from TM3 and partially fills the empty Na1 site in the apo form.
source: Within the NMD motif, the side chain of Asn310 rotates away from TM3 and partially fills the empty Na1 site, while the side chain of Met311 undergoes an opposite movement, flipping away from the binding sites (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4

claim: In the apo form, the side chain of Met311 undergoes an opposite movement to Asn310, flipping away from the binding sites.
source: Within the NMD motif, the side chain of Asn310 rotates away from TM3 and partially fills the empty Na1 site, while the side chain of Met311 undergoes an opposite movement, flipping away from the binding sites (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4

claim: TM3 bends away from the NMD motif in the apo form, particularly around Thr92 and Ser93.
source: Finally, TM3 bends away from the NMD motif, particularly around Thr92 and Ser93 (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3B,C

claim: Thr92 and Ser93 together with the side chain of Asn310 form one of the proposed third Na+-binding sites.
source: Notably, these residues together with the side chain of Asn310 form one of the proposed third Na+-binding sites (Huang and Tajkhorshid, 2010; Bastug et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous computational studies

claim: All known ligand-binding sites are distorted in the apo forms.
source: Thus, all known ligand-binding sites are distorted in the apo forms (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4

claim: The overall structures of the apo transport domain remain as closed and compacted as in the fully bound forms.
source: The overall structures of the apo transport domain remain as closed and compacted as in the fully bound forms (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The unloaded transport domains traverse the membrane as rigid bodies as deduced previously for the fully loaded transport domains.
source: Therefore, we propose that the unloaded transport domains traverse the membrane as rigid bodies as deduced previously for the fully loaded transport domains (Reyes et al., 2009).
evidence: Hypothesis based on compact structure of apo domain and previous work

claim: In GltPh, cooperative binding of Na+ ions and L-asp is central to tightly coupled transport of the solutes.
source: In GltPh, cooperative binding of Na+ ions and L-asp is central to tightly coupled transport of the solutes (Reyes et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reyes et al., 2013

claim: Binding of L-asp and Na+ at the Na2 site is coupled because the same structural element, the tip of HP2, contributes to both sites and is restructured upon binding.
source: Our structures of the apo and fully bound GltPh suggest that binding of L-asp and Na+ at the Na2 site is coupled because the same structural element, the tip of HP2, contributes to both sites and is restructured upon binding.
evidence: Inference from structural data showing HP2 involvement in both sites

claim: Structural changes in HP2 upon binding of either L-asp or Na+ should greatly favor binding of the other.
source: Thus, structural changes in HP2 upon binding of either L-asp or Na+ ion should greatly favor binding of the other.
evidence: Inference from structural coupling mechanism

claim: Met311 in the NMD motif is the only residue that is shared between the Na1 site and the substrate and Na2 sites and also undergoes a conformational change upon ligand binding.
source: Met311 in the NMD motif is the only residue that is shared between the Na1 site and the substrate and Na2 sites and also undergoes a conformational change upon ligand binding.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis

claim: The conformational changes in HP2 and the NMD motif must be concerted.
source: In both models, the side chain of Met311 clashes with residues in HP2, suggesting that the conformational changes in HP2 and the NMD motif must be concerted.
evidence: Inference from molecular modeling showing steric clashes

claim: M311A mutation reduces binding cooperativity between the substrate and Na+ ions.
source: The most parsimonious interpretation of these results is that M311A mutation reduces binding cooperativity between the substrate and Na+ ions.
evidence: Interpretation of functional data from binding assays

claim: Mutating the equivalent methionine to smaller residues in EAAT3 resulted in less steep dependence of the ionic currents on Na+ concentration.
source: Mutating the equivalent methionine to smaller residues in EAAT3 also resulted in less steep dependence of the ionic currents on Na+ concentration (Rosental and Kanner, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rosental and Kanner, 2010

claim: Met311 is key to the allosteric coupling between the Na1, L-asp and Na2 sites.
source: Based on these results, we hypothesize that Met311 is key to the allosteric coupling between the Na1, L-asp and Na2 sites.
evidence: Hypothesis based on structural and functional data

claim: Bulky methionine or leucine residues are found at position 311 in ∼85% of glutamate transporter homologues.
source: Consistently, bulky methionine or leucine residues are found at this position in ∼85% of glutamate transporter homologues.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis

claim: Methionine is conserved in the Na+-coupled GltPh and EAATs, while a characterized proton-coupled homologue has leucine at this position.
source: However, it should be noted that methionine is conserved in the Na+-coupled GltPh and EAATs, while a characterized proton-coupled homologue has leucine at this position (Gaillard et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by sequence comparison and citation

claim: It is possible that the methionine thioether plays a direct role in Na+ binding.
source: Hence, it is possible that the methionine thioether, which is proximal to both Na1 and Na2 sites, plays a direct role in Na+ binding.
evidence: Speculation based on structural position and chemical properties

claim: Binding of an ion at Na1 site should prime the transporter to accept its substrate.
source: Our hypothesis further predicts that binding of an ion at Na1 site should prime the transporter to accept its substrate.
evidence: Prediction from the proposed coupling mechanism

claim: The structure of Tl+-bound GltPhin is indistinguishable from the fully bound GltPhin.
source: Indeed, the structure of Tl+-bound GltPhin is indistinguishable from the fully bound GltPhin and both Na1 and Na2 sites are occupied by Tl+ ions (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 6A

claim: Both Na1 and Na2 sites are occupied by Tl+ ions in Tl+-bound GltPhin.
source: Indeed, the structure of Tl+-bound GltPhin is indistinguishable from the fully bound GltPhin and both Na1 and Na2 sites are occupied by Tl+ ions (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by anomalous difference Fourier map shown in Figure 6A

claim: The structure of Na+-bound GltPh-R397A differs significantly from the fully bound GltPh-R397A only at the tip of HP2.
source: The structure of Na+-bound GltPh-R397A differs significantly from the fully bound GltPh-R397A only at the tip of HP2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, also see below).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: The coordinating residues at the Na1 site are correctly positioned in Na+-bound GltPh-R397A and the site is likely occupied by a Na+ ion.
source: The coordinating residues at the Na1 site are correctly positioned and the site is likely occupied by a Na+ ion.
evidence: Inference from structural analysis

claim: The Na2 site still shows a distorted geometry in Na+-bound GltPh-R397A.
source: The Na2 site still shows a distorted geometry: the last helical turn of HP2a points away from the site due to the altered conformation of the tip of HP2 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 6C

claim: Binding of the coupled ions, notably at the Na1 site, is sufficient to trigger isomerization of the transport domain from the apo conformation to the bound-like conformation.
source: Collectively, our results demonstrate that binding of the coupled ions, notably at the Na1 site, is sufficient to trigger isomerization of the transport domain from the apo conformation to the bound-like conformation.
evidence: Conclusion from structural comparison of apo, Na+-bound, and fully bound forms

claim: The energetic penalty associated with isomerization from apo to bound-like conformation likely explains why Na+ ions alone bind weakly to the transporter.
source: The energetic penalty associated with this isomerization likely explains why Na+ ions alone bind weakly to the transporter (Reyes et al., 2013).
evidence: Inference from structural data and previous functional studies

claim: This experimental observation contrasts with highly favorable calculated binding energies that were obtained using fully bound protein conformation.
source: This experimental observation contrasts with highly favorable calculated binding energies (approximately −10 kcal/mol for Na1) that were obtained using fully bound protein conformation and where the reference ion-free state is the same as the bound state (Larsson et al., 2010; Bastug et al., 2012; Heinzelmann et al., 2013).
evidence: Comparison with previous computational studies

claim: The structure of the Na+-only bound GltPh-R397A shows HP2 in a conformation overall similar to that observed in the fully bound transporter, but with an opened tip.
source: The structure of the Na+-only bound GltPh-R397A shows HP2 in a conformation overall similar to that observed in the fully bound transporter, but with an opened tip (Figure 6B–D,F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in figures

claim: The opening of HP2 tip in Na+-bound GltPh-R397A is smaller than the opening observed previously in the structure of GltPh in complex with the blocker L-threo-β-benzyloxyaspartate.
source: This opening is smaller than the opening observed previously in the structure of GltPh in complex with the blocker L-threo-β-benzyloxyaspartate (Figure 6—figure supplement 2; Boudker et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by comparison to previous structure

claim: The HP2 tip opening is hinged at two well-conserved glycine residues at positions 351 and 357.
source: and it is hinged at two well-conserved glycine residues at positions 351 and 357 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 6C

claim: Among the nine amino acids forming the tip in GltPh, five are glycines in the consensus sequence generated for the glutamate transporter family.
source: Interestingly, among the nine amino acids forming the tip in GltPh (residues 351 to 359), five are glycines in the consensus sequence generated for the glutamate transporter family, although not all are present in each homologue (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6E

claim: The glycines support the structural flexibility of the HP2 tip in all members of the family.
source: We suggest that the glycines support the structural flexibility of the HP2 tip in all members of the family, but that the structural specifics of the tip opening may vary among homologues.
evidence: Hypothesis based on sequence conservation and structural properties

claim: The structural specifics of the tip opening may vary among homologues.
source: We suggest that the glycines support the structural flexibility of the HP2 tip in all members of the family, but that the structural specifics of the tip opening may vary among homologues.
evidence: Speculation based on sequence variation

claim: The intermediate state with the opened tip of HP2 can be achieved without major steric clashes.
source: We find that such intermediate state with the opened tip of HP2 can be achieved without major steric clashes, while further progression of the transport domain to the inward-facing position could be impeded because the tip is likely to clash with TM5 in the trimerization domain (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by molecular modeling shown in Figure 7B

claim: Further progression of the transport domain to the inward-facing position could be impeded because the tip is likely to clash with TM5 in the trimerization domain.
source: We find that such intermediate state with the opened tip of HP2 can be achieved without major steric clashes, while further progression of the transport domain to the inward-facing position could be impeded because the tip is likely to clash with TM5 in the trimerization domain (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by molecular modeling shown in Figure 7B

claim: In the inward-facing state HP2 is packed against the trimerization domain and cannot open in a manner observed in the outward-facing state.
source: Also in the inward-facing state HP2 is packed against the trimerization domain and cannot open in a manner observed in the outward-facing state.
evidence: Inference from structural constraints

claim: HP2 is closed in GltPhin bound to Tl+.
source: Consistently, HP2 is closed in GltPhin bound to Tl+ (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Opening of the HP2 tip upon Na+ binding in the outward-facing state may serve as a structural mechanism preventing uncoupled uptake of Na+ ions.
source: Therefore, opening of the HP2 tip upon Na+ binding in the outward-facing state may serve as a structural mechanism preventing uncoupled uptake of Na+ ions.
evidence: Hypothesis based on structural observations and transport requirements

claim: The structural changes in the NMD motif and HP2 that are triggered upon Na+ binding at the Na1 site may lead to the loss of direct interactions between the tip of HP2 and the rest of the transport domain, resulting in tip opening.
source: We suggest that the structural changes in the NMD motif and HP2 that are triggered upon Na+ binding at the Na1 site may lead to the loss of direct interactions between the tip of HP2 and the rest of the transport domain, resulting in tip opening.
evidence: Hypothesis based on structural analysis

claim: Subsequent binding of L-asp and Na+ at the Na2 site is required to provide compensatory interactions, allowing HP2 tip to close.
source: Subsequent binding of L-asp and Na+ at the Na2 site is then required to provide compensatory interactions, allowing HP2 tip to close.
evidence: Hypothesis based on structural analysis

claim: Similar conformational behavior has been observed for transporters with the LeuT fold: when bound to Na+ ions only, substrate binding sites are open to the extracellular solution, and substrate binding is required for occlusion.
source: Similar conformational behavior has been observed for transporters with the LeuT fold: when bound to Na+ ions only, substrate binding sites are open to the extracellular solution, and substrate binding is required for occlusion (Weyand et al., 2008; Krishnamurthy and Gouaux, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on other transporters

claim: The measured dissociation constant for Na+ ions in the inward-facing state is 250 mM.

claim: Na+ concentration in the cytoplasm is 10 mM.

claim: Na+-bound inward-facing state is not expected to be significantly populated.

claim: Transition intermediates mediate fluxes of polar solutes, including anions, because potentially hydrated cavities form in such intermediates at the interface between the trimerization and transport domains.
source: We and others have proposed that transition intermediates mediate fluxes of polar solutes, including anions, because potentially hydrated cavities form in such intermediates at the interface between the trimerization and transport domains (Stolzenberg et al., 2012; Verdon and Boudker, 2012; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous proposals

claim: Opening of the tip in the Na+-only bound form may increase solvent accessibility to the interface between trimerization and transport domains.
source: Interestingly, because the tip of HP2 forms part of this interface in the fully bound intermediate state of the transporter, opening of the tip in the Na+-only bound form may increase solvent accessibility to the interface (Figure 7A).
evidence: Speculation based on structural analysis shown in Figure 7A

claim: In approximately one third of apo GltPhin crystals soaked in Tl+, Tl+ ions bound to the Na1 and Na2 sites, inducing transition from apo- to bound-like conformation.
source: While soaking apo GltPhin crystals in Tl+ solutions, we observed that only in approximately one third of crystals Tl+ ions bound to the Na1 and Na2 sites, inducing transition from apo- to bound-like conformation as described above.
evidence: Observation from crystallographic experiments

claim: In the majority of apo GltPhin crystals soaked in Tl+, no conformational changes of the transport domain were observed and Tl+ ions incorporated at two previously uncharacterized sites.
source: In the majority of the crystals, we observed no conformational changes of the transport domain and Tl+ ions incorporated at two previously uncharacterized sites (Figure 8)
evidence: Observation from crystallographic experiments shown in Figure 8

claim: One new Tl+ binding site, termed Na2', involves residues of HP2 and TM7a that form the Na2 site, but in a different ion coordinating geometry due to the conformational difference in HP2.
source: One site, termed Na2', involves residues of HP2 and TM7a that form the Na2 site, but in a different ion coordinating geometry due to the conformational difference in HP2 (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 8B

claim: The second new site, termed Ct, overlaps with the L-asp binding site and is formed by the side chains of highly conserved Asp394 and Thr398 in TM8 and main chain carbonyl oxygen atoms of HP1 and HP2.
source: The second site, termed Ct, overlaps with the L-asp binding site and is formed by the side chains of highly conserved Asp394 and Thr398 in TM8 and main chain carbonyl oxygen atoms of HP1 and HP2 (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 8B,C

claim: Tl+ soaks of the outward-facing apo GltPh-R397A showed no conformational changes of the transport domain, with Tl+ binding at the Ct site, but not at the Na2' site.
source: Tl+ soaks of the outward-facing apo GltPh-R397A also showed no conformational changes of the transport domain, with Tl+ binding at the Ct site, but not at the Na2' site (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 8A

claim: The ion selectivity of the Ct site remains ambiguous, because neither 300 mM K+ nor 10 mM Na+ efficiently inhibited incorporation of Tl+ at this site in GltPhin.
source: The ion selectivity of the Ct site remains ambiguous, because neither 300 mM K+ nor 10 mM Na+ efficiently inhibited incorporation of Tl+ (150 mM) at this site in GltPhin (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by competition experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2

claim: The Na2' site seems to show a preference for Na+, which even at low concentration interfered significantly with Tl+ binding.
source: In contrast, the Na2' site seems to show a preference for Na+, which even at low concentration (10 mM) interfered significantly with Tl+ binding.
evidence: Supported by competition experiments

claim: The Ct site is positioned exactly at the same place as the amino group of the bound L-asp and shares several coordinating moieties.
source: However, it is remarkable that the Ct site is positioned exactly at the same place as the amino group of the bound L-asp and share several coordinating moieties.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison

claim: Binding of a cation at the Ct site and binding of the substrate are mutually exclusive.
source: Therefore, binding of a cation at the Ct site and binding of the substrate are mutually exclusive.
evidence: Inference from structural overlap

claim: Cation binding at the Ct site would inhibit the transition into the bound-like conformation upon Na+ binding at the Na1 site.
source: Because the Ct site is observed only in the apo-like conformation, cation binding at this site would also inhibit the transition into the bound-like conformation upon Na+ binding at the Na1 site.
evidence: Inference from structural observations

claim: The Ct site is observed in both the inward- and outward-facing states.
source: Finally, the Ct site is observed in both the inward- and outward-facing states, suggesting that the apo-like transport domain could carry the ion across the membrane.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data

claim: The apo-like transport domain could carry the ion bound at the Ct site across the membrane.
source: Finally, the Ct site is observed in both the inward- and outward-facing states, suggesting that the apo-like transport domain could carry the ion across the membrane.
evidence: Inference from structural observations

claim: It has been previously proposed that K+ binds to EAATs at a similar position to the Ct site.
source: Moreover, it has been previously proposed that K+ binds to EAATs at a similar position (Holley and Kavanaugh, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Holley and Kavanaugh, 2009

claim: In an insect K+-independent dicarboxylate transporter, an asparagine to aspartate mutation at the position equivalent to Asp394 in GltPh changes the transporter substrate specificity to amino acid glutamate, and also leads to dependence on K+ counter-transport.
source: Most remarkably, in an insect K+-independent dicarboxylate transporter, an asparagine to aspartate mutation at the position equivalent to Asp394 in GltPh changes the transporter substrate specificity to amino acid glutamate, and also leads to dependence on K+ counter-transport (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2013

claim: Asp394 plays a key role in both binding the amino group of substrate and coupling to K+ counter-transport.
source: Therefore this aspartate plays a key role in both binding the amino group of substrate and coupling to K+ counter-transport.
evidence: Inference from mutagenesis data in related transporter

claim: Asp394 in GltPh coordinates both the amino group of the bound substrate and Tl+ in the Ct site.
source: Consistently, Asp394 in GltPh coordinates both the amino group of the bound substrate and Tl+ in the Ct site.
evidence: Supported by structural data

claim: While Tl+ mimics, to some extent, Na+ ions in GltPh and EAATs, it is a better mimic of K+ ions in EAATs.
source: Notably, while Tl+ mimics, to some extent, Na+ ions in GltPh and EAATs, it is a better mimic of K+ ions in EAATs (Boudker et al., 2007; Tao et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: In alkali-free GltPhin, HP1 and TM7a moved slightly towards TM8, with the tip of HP1 detaching from that of HP2.
source: Interestingly, we observed a small, but reproducible structural change in several crystals examined: HP1 and TM7a that form the transport domain cytoplasmic surface moved slightly towards TM8, with the tip of HP1 detaching from that of HP2 (Figure 9, Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 9

claim: The movement of HP1 in alkali-free GltPhin is reminiscent of the isomerization of the structurally symmetric HP2 and TM8a on the extracellular side of the domain observed upon the transition from bound to apo forms.
source: This movement is observed clearly in one protomer (chain B in 4P3J), in which these helices are not involved in crystal packing contacts. It is reminiscent of the isomerization of the structurally symmetric HP2 and TM8a on the extracellular side of the domain observed upon the transition from bound to apo forms (Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 9B

claim: It was suggested previously that HP1 participates in intracellular gating in GltPh.
source: It was suggested previously that HP1 participates in intracellular gating in GltPh (Reyes et al., 2009; DeChancie et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The observed movement of HP1 generates a small opening, leading to the substrate and Ct sites.
source: Indeed, the observed movement of HP1 generates a small opening, leading to the substrate and Ct sites (Figure 9—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2

claim: The movement of HP1 is reminiscent of the movement observed in molecular dynamics simulations.
source: and it is reminiscent of the movement observed in molecular dynamics simulations (DeChancie et al., 2010; Zomot and Bahar, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to computational studies

claim: Ion binding and unbinding events in GltPh and EAATs control the conformational state of the transporter, determining its competence to bind substrate and undergo transitions between the outward- and inward-facing states.
source: In conclusion, we have shown structurally that ion binding and unbinding events in GltPh and, by analogy, in EAATs control the conformational state of the transporter, determining its competence to bind substrate and undergo transitions between the outward- and inward-facing states.
evidence: Summary conclusion from structural data

claim: Local conformational changes within the transport domain accompany binding and release of the transported substrate and ions.
source: Our apo and ions-only bound structures reveal a remarkable structural plasticity of GltPh transport domain that is likely a conserved feature in the glutamate transporter family. In addition to the large trans-membrane rigid-body movements of the transport domain between outward- and inward-facing orientations, local conformational changes within the domain accompany binding and release of the transported substrate and ions (Figure 10).
evidence: Supported by structural data summarized in Figure 10

claim: These local changes provide a structural explanation of how Na+ gradients are harnessed to drive concentrative substrate uptake.
source: These local changes provide a structural explanation of how Na+ gradients are harnessed to drive concentrative substrate uptake, supporting two previously proposed coupling mechanisms (Focke et al., 2011; Reyes et al., 2013): allosterically coupled binding of the substrate and symported Na+ ions, and opening of HP2 upon Na+ binding, which impedes the inward trans-membrane movement of the Na+-only bound transport domain.
evidence: Interpretation of structural data in context of transport mechanism

claim: The structural data support allosterically coupled binding of the substrate and symported Na+ ions as a coupling mechanism.
source: These local changes provide a structural explanation of how Na+ gradients are harnessed to drive concentrative substrate uptake, supporting two previously proposed coupling mechanisms (Focke et al., 2011; Reyes et al., 2013): allosterically coupled binding of the substrate and symported Na+ ions, and opening of HP2 upon Na+ binding, which impedes the inward trans-membrane movement of the Na+-only bound transport domain.
evidence: Interpretation of structural data in context of previous proposals

claim: The structural data support opening of HP2 upon Na+ binding, which impedes the inward trans-membrane movement of the Na+-only bound transport domain, as a coupling mechanism.
source: These local changes provide a structural explanation of how Na+ gradients are harnessed to drive concentrative substrate uptake, supporting two previously proposed coupling mechanisms (Focke et al., 2011; Reyes et al., 2013): allosterically coupled binding of the substrate and symported Na+ ions, and opening of HP2 upon Na+ binding, which impedes the inward trans-membrane movement of the Na+-only bound transport domain.
evidence: Interpretation of structural data in context of previous proposals

claim: The transport domains continuously sample the outward- and inward-facing positions with nearly equal probabilities either when bound to Na+ and L-asp or when free of the solutes.
source: Consistently, previous spectroscopic studies showed that the transport domains continuously sample the outward- and inward-facing positions with nearly equal probabilities either when bound to Na+ and L-asp or when free of the solutes (Akyuz et al., 2013; Erkens et al., 2013; Georgieva et al., 2013; Hanelt et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to spectroscopic studies

claim: Transitions between outward- and inward-facing positions are more frequent in the apo transporter, consistent with a lack of large energetic barriers.
source: Moreover, these transitions are more frequent in the apo transporter, consistent with a lack of large energetic barriers (Akyuz et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to spectroscopic study

claim: In GltPh, the compact translocation-competent apo conformation of the transport domain is stabilized by interactions between the collapsed HP2, and HP1, TM7, and TM8.
source: In GltPh, the compact translocation-competent apo conformation of the transport domain is stabilized by interactions between the collapsed HP2, and HP1, TM7, and TM8.
evidence: Inference from structural analysis

claim: In EAATs, interactions stabilizing the apo conformation are insufficient and K+ binding to the Ct site is required to stabilize the translocation-competent closed conformation.
source: In EAATs, by contrast, we speculate that these interactions are insufficient and that K+ binding to the Ct site is required to stabilize the translocation-competent closed conformation that can return to the outside, ensuring coupling between substrate uptake and counter-transport of K+ ion.
evidence: Speculation based on structural data and functional differences

claim: K+ binding to the Ct site ensures coupling between substrate uptake and counter-transport of K+ ion in EAATs.
source: In EAATs, by contrast, we speculate that these interactions are insufficient and that K+ binding to the Ct site is required to stabilize the translocation-competent closed conformation that can return to the outside, ensuring coupling between substrate uptake and counter-transport of K+ ion.
evidence: Speculation based on structural data and functional differences

claim: Local structural differences in EAATs in the vicinity of the Ct site may underlie the higher affinity and specificity of this site for K+ ion.
